raw_evidence.quote:
Each key of a SQL Table shape defines a row. The primary value (the thing after the colon) of each row defines its type.

The constraint value of each row defines its SQL constraint. D2 will recognize and shorten:

| constraint  | short |
| ----------- | ----- |
| primary_key | PK    |
| foreign_key | FK    |
| unique      | UNQ   |

But you can set any constraint you'd like. It just won't be shortened if unrecognized.

You can also specify multiple constraints with an array.

```d2
x: int { constraint: [primary_key; unique] }
```

raw_evidence.locator: static/d2/tables-2.d2 (embedded verbatim in docs/tour/sql-tables.md "Foreign Keys" section)

composite_primary_keys.citation: docs/tour/sql-tables.md "Basics" section (constraint table + 'any constraint you'd like' sentence) plus open issue d2lang/d2#671
composite_primary_keys.rationale: The `constraint` field is declared per single row (column) and is either shortened to PK/FK/UNQ if recognized or passed through as free text. There is no documented syntax that groups two or more columns into one joint PK/UNQ/FK constraint. The 'array' syntax (`constraint: [primary_key; unique]`) applies MULTIPLE distinct constraint labels to ONE column, not one constraint spanning multiple columns — a different feature entirely, easy to mistake for composite-key support. Maintainers' own open feature request #671 confirms directly: 'd2 can't represent FKs that are composed of more than one column' and shows a workaround-free example where the author wants `(id, tenant)` as a joint PK and has no syntax to write it. Two columns each individually labelled `primary_key` would render as two separate PK badges with no indication they are jointly one constraint — a rendering artifact, not an expressed constraint. Verdict: not-expressible, not even via workaround, since no combination of documented syntax produces a joint multi-column constraint.

json_payload_columns.citation: docs/tour/sql-tables.md "Foreign Keys" example, tables-2.d2, column `json: jsonb`
json_payload_columns.rationale: The row's type slot is free text — `jsonb` is used in the official example, so a column CAN be labelled with a JSON-ish type string and it will render. But the type slot carries no semantics: D2 does not parse, validate, or distinguish 'jsonb' from any other string; it is decorative text in a table row, identical in kind to `int` or the non-standard `blob` used in tables-3.d2 (blob is not a real SQL type, and D2 accepts it without complaint because nothing checks it). So a JSON payload column can be drawn, but the language attaches no meaning to 'this column holds an opaque JSON document' beyond what a human reads off the label — hence workaround-only, not true type semantics.

enumerated_string_domains.citation: docs/tour/sql-tables.md "Basics" section — absence of any enum/domain construct in the documented row grammar (type slot + single constraint slot only)
enumerated_string_domains.rationale: The row grammar has exactly two semantic slots: type (free text) and constraint (free text, optionally shortened if PK/FK/UNQ). No documented mechanism restricts a column's legal values to an enumerated set. A modeller could put the literal string `SCHEDULED|MANUAL` in the type slot as a label, but D2 would not enforce, parse, or check it — same free-text-label ceiling as JSON columns. No CHECK-constraint or enum construct is mentioned anywhere on this page or the constraint table.

self_referencing_foreign_keys.citation: docs/tour/sql-tables.md "Foreign Keys" section — the connection syntax `objects.disk -> disks.id`
self_referencing_foreign_keys.rationale: Nothing in the shown syntax restricts the connection's source and target table to be different tables — `some_table.col_a -> some_table.col_b` would parse identically to any other row-to-row connection, so three self-referencing FKs on one table can be drawn as three separate connections. But each connection is a generic D2 edge (the same primitive used for connecting arbitrary shapes anywhere in the language) with no FK-specific semantics: nothing associates the connection with the `constraint: foreign_key` label on the source column, nothing prevents a connection with no matching constraint label, and nothing distinguishes which of the several outgoing connections corresponds to which self-referencing column beyond the reader's own visual tracing. It draws the right picture but the FK-ness is purely conventional/visual, hence workaround, not genuine relational semantics.

nullable_foreign_keys.citation: docs/tour/sql-tables.md "Basics" section — constraint table lists only primary_key/foreign_key/unique; no null/not-null keyword documented
nullable_foreign_keys.rationale: There is no documented constraint keyword for nullability (no 'nullable', 'not null', 'required', or similar in the recognized-and-shortened table, and no mention elsewhere on the page). A modeller could invent an unrecognized constraint string like `constraint: nullable`, which the docs confirm will render unshortened as free text — but that is indistinguishable, to the language, from a typo or an arbitrary label. Not-expressible as a checked property; at best a decorative label with the same status as any made-up word.

multi_column_unique_constraints.citation: docs/tour/sql-tables.md "Basics" section (constraint table + 'array' info box) plus open issue d2lang/d2#671/#672
multi_column_unique_constraints.rationale: Same structural gap as composite primary keys: `unique` is a per-row (single-column) constraint label. The array syntax lets one column carry multiple DIFFERENT constraint kinds (e.g. both primary_key and unique on the same column) but does not let two columns jointly form one unique constraint. No documented syntax names a constraint that spans columns.

one_to_zero_or_one_relationships.citation: docs/tour/sql-tables.md "Foreign Keys" example (plain `->` connection); see companion record source-d2-sql-table-generation.json for the arrowhead-style documentation citation
one_to_zero_or_one_relationships.rationale: D2 connections support crow's-foot-style arrowheads (cf-one, cf-one-required, cf-many, cf-many-required — documented on the connections/arrowheads page) which can be applied to a connection between two sql_table rows to make it LOOK like a one-to-zero-or-one relationship. But arrowhead choice is purely a rendering/styling attribute of the connection primitive — it is not interpreted by the compiler as a cardinality constraint the way a foreign-key or check constraint would be. The sql-tables.md page itself documents only the plain `->` connection with no cardinality vocabulary. Verdict: the visual notation exists as a styling choice, but it carries no enforced or checked cardinality semantics — expressible only as a picture, not as a constraint.

value_constraint_beyond_type.citation: docs/tour/sql-tables.md "Basics" section — row grammar has only type + constraint slots, neither of which supports a value expression (e.g. CHECK, range, or literal-alternation)
value_constraint_beyond_type.rationale: There is no documented way to say a column holds 'a decimal positive integer OR the literal ALL' beyond writing that phrase as the free-text type string, which — per the same reasoning as JSON columns and enums — is rendered as an uninterpreted label. No CHECK-constraint syntax, no value-expression grammar, is documented anywhere in the sql_table shape reference.

contrary_evidence_search.result: Found direct, maintainer-acknowledged confirmation of the composite-key gap: open issue d2lang/d2#671 ('[FR] sql_table: Support PK and FK composed by 2+ attributes', opened 2023-01-16, still open) states plainly 'At the moment d2 can't represent FKs that are composed of more than one column.' Related open issues #672 ('sql_table: support multiple constraints on columns') and #1386 ('d2oracle: set on sql_table columns constraint should be maps') corroborate that the constraint model is a simple per-column label list, not a constraint-object model. Search for 'enum' or 'check constraint' in the issue tracker returned no results relevant to sql_table (only unrelated hits about label alignment and URL encoding), consistent with the documentation's silence on enums/CHECK constraints — read here as absence of the feature rather than absence of demand, since no docs page, changelog, or issue proposes it either way.
